name: Ostrogothic Kingdom
summary: A Gothic kingdom in Italy founded by Theodoric the Great, who ruled Goths and Romans side by side from Ravenna; Byzantium destroyed it in the Gothic War (535–554).

knownFor.label: Boethius
knownFor.note: Wrote the Consolation of Philosophy in prison.

location.value: Italy and neighbouring areas (493–553); the capital was Ravenna.

terrain.value: The Italian peninsula, with the Po plain in the north, the Apennine mountains and long coasts.

climate.value: Mediterranean in most of Italy, cooler and wetter in the north.

resources.value: Grain, wine, olive oil, timber and the rich farmland of the Po valley.

disasters.value: The plague of Justinian reached the empire in 541, though its worst effects in Italy came after the kingdom had fallen.

population.value: Several million Romans and about 100,000 Goths.

urbanisation.value: Roman cities such as Ravenna, Rome, Verona.

disease.value: The first great plague pandemic (from 541) spread across the Mediterranean, probably reaching Italy by 543.

migration.value: Goths moved from the Balkans to Italy (489).

economicBase.value: Farming on Roman-style estates (villas), supported by Roman taxes and some trade.

tradeRoutes.value: The Mediterranean trade network continued through Italian ports such as Ravenna and Ostia.

wealth.value: Great Roman landowning families kept much of the wealth; the Gothic kings also gained from taxes.

moneyAndTax.value: Roman gold and silver coins and the Roman tax system continued; Theodoric’s coins still carried the emperor’s name.

governmentType.value: A Germanic monarchy that kept the Roman administration, its senior officials and the Senate.

keyRulers.value: Theodoric the Great (493–526); Amalasuntha, regent for her son Athalaric; Witiges; Totila.

succession.value: Kings came from the Amal family, but after Theodoric’s death in 526 the succession was often disputed.

stability.value: Stable under Theodoric; the execution of Boethius (524) showed growing tension; then war from 535.

eliteConflict.value: Pro-Byzantine and anti-Byzantine factions among the Goths and Romans, which also divided the royal family.

armyAndTech.value: Gothic cavalry formed the core of the army, while Romans ran government and the law.

majorWars.value: The Gothic War against Justinian’s Byzantine Empire (535–553), ending with defeats at Taginae and Mons Lactarius.

alliancesRivals.value: The Byzantine Empire, the Franks, and the Visigoths, who helped Theodoric against Odoacer (490).

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; Cassiodorus helped preserve classical learning.

scienceEducation.value: Roman officials and scholars such as Boethius served the court; Boethius was executed in 524.

openness.value: Goths and Romans lived side by side with separate laws and, often, different religions.

communicationTransport.value: The Roman road network, Ravenna’s harbour and the postal system continued to function.

religion.value: The Goths were mostly Homoian (“Arian”) Christians; the Romans were Catholic (Nicene).

languageWriting.value: Latin was used for government and the Church; the Goths spoke Gothic, which survives only in a few texts such as Wulfila’s Bible.

artsArchitecture.value: The Basilica of Sant’Apollinare Nuovo and its mosaics, and the Mausoleum of Theodoric in Ravenna.

socialStructure.value: The Goths settled mostly in northern Italy and kept apart from the Roman population.

sharedIdentity.value: Goths and Romans kept separate identities, though Theodoric tried to bring them together.

dailyLife.value: Roman-style town life and farming went on, with Goths mostly settled on lands as soldiers.

ideasReligions.value: Classical learning survived under Theodoric’s officials, such as Boethius and Cassiodorus; the Goths were Arian Christians while most Romans were Catholic.

colonisation.value: The Goths took over Roman Italy in 493 with the agreement of the Eastern emperor.

riseSignals.value: Theodoric the Great defeated and killed Odoacer and took Ravenna (493).

peakPeriod.value: Theodoric the Great’s reign (493–526), a time of peace and building in Ravenna.

declineSignals.value: The Byzantine invasion of 535 began the long Gothic War, which ended Ostrogothic rule by 553.

outcome.value: Conquered by the Byzantines (553); the weakened Byzantines then lost much of Italy to the Lombards (568).

overallCertainty.value: Well documented by Procopius and Cassiodorus.
